title: Flexible Pages: Build Plan
eyebrow: Build plan for your approval · four steps · issues #541 to #545 · no code written yet

short.lead: You approved the design: any page format, if it meets seven basics. This is how I build it, in four steps. Each step is one issue and ends with a check I run and show you. Your part: answer two choices, then approve.
short.hint: Tap a step to see what it builds.
items: I write a page and it is not refused for being hand-made

The page check stops asking whether the builder made the page. It asks whether the page meets the basics. A good hand-made page goes through. A page that misses a basic is refused once, with the basic named.

items.alt: A page with the builder mark is allowed as today. A page without it is read by a new checker and allowed if the basics are met, or refused once naming each failed basic.
items.caption: Blue exists today. Green is new. A plain diagram.

items: The page check is one small test

event_pagecheck in design_loop.py allows a page only if its first 4096 characters hold the builder mark. The builder's template has four fixed parts. Nothing reads what a page contains. I reuse that hook and the builder's phone-width check; I add one script and change one test.
The two choices below are about how the checker finds things on a page.

changes: A script that reads one page and prints each failed basic in plain words. It looks for a summary, a next-step box, a picture, steps, a checklist, blocks over 60 words outside folded detail, and runs the existing phone-width check. Planned shape: check(html, type) returns a list of messages; main prints them and exits 1 on any. Tested by new verify.py cases: one passing page per type, one failing page per basic.
One script lists each failed basic.
Done when the new cases and the full verify.py pass.
Step 2 (#543): the page check reads, not refuses

A page without the builder mark goes to the checker instead of straight to refusal. Pass: allowed. Fail: refused once with the failed basics named. Pages with the mark pass as today. A project's docs/page-style.json may add stricter limits. The existing verify.py cases that expect any unmarked page to be refused are updated.
Any page without the mark is refused.
A page that meets the basics is allowed.
Done when a good hand-made page is written freely and a bad one is refused with the reason.

A content skeleton for proposal, build plan, QA, review and art, each built on the basics. make_page.py can start from one. The builder's own template gains a next-step box that stays on screen, so builder pages meet the basics too. Using a starter is optional.
A starter per type, or no starter.
Done when a page from each starter passes the checker.
Step 4 (#545): rules, docs, version, QA page

The rule text names the basics and the types. The injected rules text has a size limit, so I cut as much as I add. I update the systems doc, state doc, Today, changelog and the plugin version, then build the QA page with the steps you follow.
Rules describe the basics and the types.
Done when verify.py passes and you say "QA passed: flexible pages".
Your words still move the stage, and the destructive-command guard, main-branch guard and credit check are untouched.
Nothing about how you approve changes.
choices: How does the checker find the next-step box and the checklist?
The page marks them with a data-basic attribute (for example data-basic="next")
Reliable, and a few characters of markup in any format. A page that forgets is told which one.
The checker guesses from the words on the page
No markup, but a good page can fail on wording and a bad one can pass.
A, because a guess that is wrong either blocks a good page or lets a bad one through.
How does a page say what type it is?
A meta tag in the page head: house-rules-page, with proposal, build-plan, qa, review or art
One line, explicit, and the checker applies that type's extra rules.
The checker infers the type from the file name and the words
Nothing to add, but it will sometimes pick the wrong type.
A, so the type is never a guess.
